title: From gas to stars along the spiral wave: CO, HCN, and star formation variations across the spiral arms in NGC 4321 and M51
comment: Accepted publication in A&A, 12 pages, 5 appendix, 15 figures
summary: Molecular clouds form stars from the interstellar medium via gravitational collapse, following a sequence from low-density gas to high-density cores and eventually the formation of stars. In classical density wave theory, gas clouds orbiting the galaxy experience gas compression and triggered star formation, while encountering the gravitational well of spiral arms. We aim to trace these different phases of the molecular cloud life cycle via tracers of molecular gas (CO), dense molecular gas (HCN), and star formation (H$α$, 24 $μ$m) within the spiral arms of two grand-design spiral galaxies: NGC 4321 and M51 (NGC 5194). In the spiral arms of these galaxies, we investigate the relation between molecular gas, dense gas, and star formation (CO-HCN-SFR) at matched physical resolutions of 270 pc and 125 pc in NGC 4321 and M51, respectively. We employed spiral arm masks for these galaxies and investigate trends of HCN/CO and SFR/HCN (SFR/CO), which serve as proxies for the dense gas fraction and dense (molecular) gas star formation efficiency, perpendicular to the spiral arm spines. We find that HCN/CO, SFR/CO, and SFR/HCN increase from the upstream towards the downstream side of both spiral arms of NGC 4321, while their trends are less prominent in M51. Our results indicate that large-scale galactic dynamics (e.g. density waves) can induce a sequence of gas density and star formation-to-gas density variations perpendicular to the spiral arms. This sequence contributes to the increased scatter seen among spectroscopic ratios such as HCN/CO and SFR/HCN at sub-kiloparsec scales.

AI.tldr: This study analyzes the CO-HCN-SFR relation across spiral arms in NGC 4321 and M51 at matched resolutions (270 pc and 125 pc), finding that HCN/CO, SFR/CO, and SFR/HCN increase from upstream to downstream sides of spiral arms in NGC 4321, with less prominent trends in M51, indicating that galactic density waves induce a sequence of gas compression and star formation perpendicular to spiral arms.
AI.motivation: To trace the molecular cloud life cycle from low-density gas to dense cores and star formation within spiral arms, and understand how large-scale galactic dynamics (density waves) influence gas density variations and star formation efficiency at sub-kiloparsec scales.
AI.method: Used spiral arm masks to investigate HCN/CO (dense gas fraction), SFR/CO, and SFR/HCN (dense gas star formation efficiency) perpendicular to spiral arm spines in NGC 4321 and M51 at matched physical resolutions of 270 pc and 125 pc, respectively.
AI.result: HCN/CO, SFR/CO, and SFR/HCN increase from upstream to downstream sides of both spiral arms in NGC 4321; trends are less prominent in M51.
AI.conclusion: Large-scale galactic dynamics, such as density waves, can induce ordered variations in gas density and star formation efficiency perpendicular to spiral arms, contributing to the scatter in spectroscopic ratios at sub-kiloparsec scales.

title: Constraints on the inflationary vacuum and reheating era from NANOGrav
comment: 22 pages, 4 captioned figures. Comments are welcome
summary: NANOGrav and various pulsar timing array experiments recently reported evidence for a common red noise signal across millisecond pulsars. This signal exhibits Hellings-Downs inter-pulsar correlation patterns, providing compelling evidence for a stochastic gravitational wave background (SGWB) signal. In general, such a background can come from several astrophysical and cosmological phenomena. Assuming such SGWB has an inflationary origin, we use latest NANOGrav 15-year dataset to constrain the inflationary parameters e.g., tensor spectral index ($n_t$), tensor-to-scalar ratio ($r$), and explore the implications for the reheating phase through constraints on the reheating equation of state ($ω_{\text{re}}$) and reheating temperature ($T_{\text{re}})$. We find the preference for an extremely blue-tilted tensor spectrum $n_t=2.20^{+0.36}_{-1.2}$ and the radiation-like reheating scenario $ω_{\text{re}}=0.33^{+0.14}_{-0.36}$. Despite having no concrete evidence for the nature of the primordial vacua, the computation of gravitational wave (GW) sourced by tensor perturbations assumes the inflationary vacuum to be a Bunch-Davies vacuum. In this work, we examine modifications to the GW spectrum originating from the non-Bunch-Davies primordial vacuum. We find that NANOGrav observations favour a specific type of non-Bunch-Davies vacuum, known as the alpha-vacuum. Furthermore, our analysis demonstrates that the observations strikingly narrow down the range of the parameter $α$ characterizing the vacua. On top of that, we find that a frequency-dependent parametrization of the vacuum parameter $α$ beyond a threshold frequency can yield a minimal solution to alleviate the blue-titled issue. Finally, we highlight the possibility of testing such frequency dependence of $α$ by probing the GW spectrum through future GW experiments.

AI.tldr: Using NANOGrav 15-year data, the paper constrains inflationary parameters (blue-tilted tensor spectrum, radiation-like reheating) and examines non-Bunch-Davies vacuum effects on the stochastic gravitational wave background, finding preference for the alpha-vacuum and a frequency-dependent vacuum parameter that alleviates the blue-tilt issue.
AI.motivation: To constrain inflationary parameters and explore the implications for reheating using NANOGrav's evidence for a stochastic gravitational wave background, and to examine modifications to the GW spectrum from non-Bunch-Davies primordial vacuum states.
AI.method: Analyzed the latest NANOGrav 15-year dataset to constrain tensor spectral index, tensor-to-scalar ratio, reheating equation of state, and reheating temperature. Extended the analysis to non-Bunch-Davies vacuum (alpha-vacuum) and introduced a frequency-dependent parametrization of the vacuum parameter.
AI.result: Found preference for a blue-tilted tensor spectrum (n_t=2.20^{+0.36}_{-1.2}) and radiation-like reheating (ω_re=0.33^{+0.14}_{-0.36}). NANOGrav favors the alpha-vacuum over Bunch-Davies, narrowly constrains α, and a frequency-dependent α beyond a threshold frequency alleviates the blue-tilt issue.
AI.conclusion: The NANOGrav data supports a specific non-Bunch-Davies vacuum (alpha-vacuum) and a frequency-dependent vacuum parameter that mitigates the blue-tilt problem. Future GW experiments could test this frequency dependence.

title: Spin Parity of Spiral Galaxies VI -- A Search for Dynamical Memory in the Spin Distribution of Galaxies in HSC WIDE Survey Regions
comment: 10 pages, 7 figures, 8 tables, and 1 machine-readable catalog
summary:
We analyzed the distribution of spin parity in spiral galaxies using the HSC DR2 data. The spiral winding parity of disk galaxies, observed as S-spiral or Z-spiral projected onto the sky plane, provides robust information on the sign of the line-of-sight component of their spin vectors, specifically whether the spin vector points toward or away from us. The distribution of 49,494 S/Z annotated spirals with spectroscopic redshift (0.05 $\le z$) was analyzed for 46,247 fiducial cubic search volumes of various sizes, 20--200 Mpc, deployed in the 3D supergalactic coordinates. We counted the number of S-spirals and Z-spirals in each cube, evaluated the binomial probability of the observed S/Z imbalance, and identified statistically anomalous cube candidates.
  The observed cumulative distribution functions for the 256 sets of cubes are in good agreement with the theoretical binomial distribution and with those obtained from 1000 Monte Carlo realizations assuming random S/Z spin assignments. The number of statistically anomalous cubes is also comparable to that expected from the random assignments. These results indicate that the spin-vector distribution of spiral galaxies is consistent with statistical randomness expected from the standard cosmological model of structure formation.

AI.tldr: Analysis of 49,494 spiral galaxies from HSC DR2 shows that the distribution of S/Z spin parity is consistent with statistical randomness, matching the standard cosmological model predictions, with no significant spatial anomalies detected across 46,247 cubic search volumes.
AI.motivation: To test whether the distribution of spin vectors (S-spiral vs Z-spiral) in spiral galaxies exhibits any statistically significant spatial anomalies or large-scale patterns that might challenge the standard cosmological model of structure formation.
AI.method: Using HSC DR2 data, 49,494 spiral galaxies with spectroscopic redshift (z≥0.05) were classified as S-spiral or Z-spiral. The analysis deployed 46,247 fiducial cubic search volumes (20–200 Mpc) in 3D supergalactic coordinates. For each cube, binomial probability of S/Z imbalance was computed, and anomalous cube candidates were identified. Results were compared to theoretical binomial distributions and 1000 Monte Carlo random realizations.
AI.result: The cumulative distribution functions for 256 cube sets agree well with the theoretical binomial distribution and with Monte Carlo random realizations. The number of statistically anomalous cubes is comparable to expectations from random assignments. No significant deviation from randomness was found.
AI.conclusion: The spin-vector distribution of spiral galaxies is consistent with statistical randomness as predicted by the standard cosmological model, supporting the current paradigm of structure formation.

title: Primordial Magnetic Fields at Cosmic Dawn: 21-cm Forecasts with HERA and SKA
summary: Primordial magnetic fields (PMFs) can enhance the abundance of low-mass halos during Cosmic Dawn by sourcing additional small-scale matter fluctuations. This enhanced small-scale power can accelerate early galaxy formation, shifting the timing of Lyman-$α$ coupling, X-ray heating, and reionization toward earlier times and imprinting correlated signatures on the global and fluctuating 21-cm signals. We extend the fast analytic framework {\tt\string zeus21} to include a physically motivated PMF contribution to the linear matter power spectrum, including radiative damping before recombination and magnetic-pressure suppression below the magnetic Jeans scale. The implementation preserves the speed and modularity of {\tt\string zeus21}, enabling efficient exploration of PMF parameter space. For $n_B=-2.9$, we quantify the impact of PMFs on early structure formation and 21-cm observables across a range of fiducial magnetic amplitudes, and forecast detectability with \textit{HERA} and \textit{SKA}. Combining 21-cm forecasts with external CMB priors, we find that upcoming experiments can probe PMFs through their impact on small-scale structure, providing constraints complementary to existing cosmological probes.

AI.tldr: This paper extends the zeus21 framework to include primordial magnetic field (PMF) effects on the matter power spectrum, showing that PMFs accelerate early structure formation and imprint detectable signatures on 21-cm signals, with HERA and SKA capable of constraining PMF amplitudes complementary to CMB bounds.
AI.motivation: To understand how primordial magnetic fields (PMFs) influence early galaxy formation and the 21-cm signal, and to enable efficient exploration of PMF parameter space using a fast analytic framework.
AI.method: The authors extend the fast analytic framework zeus21 to include a physically motivated PMF contribution to the linear matter power spectrum, accounting for radiative damping before recombination and magnetic-pressure suppression below the magnetic Jeans scale, while preserving the speed and modularity of the original code.
AI.result: For a spectral index n_B = -2.9, the authors quantify how PMFs enhance low-mass halo abundance, accelerate Lyman-α coupling, X-ray heating, and reionization, and produce correlated 21-cm signatures. Forecasts show HERA and SKA can detect these signatures, and combining with CMB priors yields complementary constraints on PMF amplitudes.
AI.conclusion: Upcoming 21-cm experiments can probe primordial magnetic fields through their impact on small-scale structure, providing constraints complementary to existing cosmological probes.

title: The formation of the C-19 progenitor: a primordial cluster heated by gas expulsion
comment: 11+4 pages, 2+2 figures, 3 tables, accepted for publication in ApJ Letters
summary: The extremely metal-poor nature of the C-19 stream indicates that its progenitor was a primordial stellar system born in the very early Universe. Current observations show that it has a small metallicity dispersion (0.18 at the 95% confidence level), which is the signature of a globular cluster origin, while at the same time displaying an unusually large velocity dispersion ($\sim10$ km/s) typical of dwarf galaxies. To reconcile this conflicting observational evidence, previous simulations have focused on potential interactions with dark matter subhalos, which can efficiently make a cluster stream dynamically hot. In this work, we explore internal dynamical processes in star cluster formation, focusing on initial conditions shaped by gas expulsion and a top-heavy initial mass function. We find that the large observed velocity dispersion and broad stream morphology can be reproduced by a cluster that underwent severe gas expulsion and expansion during its birth phase, which is potentially a typical formation scenario of extremely metal-poor star clusters. A top-heavy IMF and binaries can also increase the velocity dispersion. The formation of C-19 may involve a combination of these effects.

AI.tldr: This study explores internal dynamical processes (gas expulsion, top-heavy IMF, binaries) as alternative explanations for the conflicting observational properties of the C-19 stream—low metallicity dispersion (globular cluster-like) but high velocity dispersion (dwarf galaxy-like)—finding that severe gas expulsion during cluster birth can reproduce the observed kinematics, potentially offering a typical formation scenario for extremely metal-poor star clusters.
AI.motivation: To reconcile conflicting observational evidence of the C-19 stream (small metallicity dispersion vs. large velocity dispersion) by exploring internal dynamical processes in star cluster formation, rather than external interactions with dark matter subhalos as previous simulations have focused on.
AI.method: Numerical simulations exploring internal dynamical processes in star cluster formation, focusing on initial conditions shaped by gas expulsion, a top-heavy initial mass function (IMF), and binary star effects.
AI.result: The large observed velocity dispersion (~10 km/s) and broad stream morphology of C-19 can be reproduced by a cluster that underwent severe gas expulsion and expansion during its birth phase. A top-heavy IMF and binaries can also increase the velocity dispersion.
AI.conclusion: The formation of C-19 may involve a combination of gas expulsion, top-heavy IMF, and binary effects. Severe gas expulsion during the birth phase is potentially a typical formation scenario of extremely metal-poor star clusters.

title: Backreaction and the Role of Spatial Curvature in the Cosmic Neighborhood
summary: We present the first direct computation of spatially averaged dynamical quantities in the local Universe, employing the Cosmicflows-4++ reconstruction and a covariant scalar averaging formalism. We extract the domain-averaged density, expansion rate, spatial curvature, and kinematical backreaction over cosmologically relevant domains around our Galaxy, extending up to a comoving radius of $300~\mathrm{Mpc}/h$. The resulting domain-averaged present-day energy budget features nontrivial variations with scale that reflect a nested structure within the cosmic neighborhood, including a large-scale void shell encompassing the local cosmic web. Remarkably, we find significant contributions to this energy budget from the average spatial curvature at the $\mathcal{O}(10\%)$ level on all probed scales. By contrast, the kinematical backreaction remains much smaller throughout the surveyed volume, reaching at most a $\mathcal{O}(1\%)$ contribution on the smallest scales considered, i.e., $30~\mathrm{Mpc}/h$. Convergence to the global $Λ$CDM background is not observed within this range of scales.

AI.tldr: This paper presents the first direct computation of spatially averaged dynamical quantities in the local Universe using Cosmicflows-4++ data and covariant scalar averaging. The domain-averaged energy budget shows significant (𝒪(10%)) spatial curvature contributions on all probed scales, while kinematical backreaction is small (𝒪(1%) on smallest scales). Convergence to ΛCDM background is not observed within 300 Mpc/h.
AI.motivation: To directly compute spatially averaged dynamical quantities in the local Universe using real observational data (Cosmicflows-4++ reconstruction) rather than relying solely on simulations or theoretical models, in order to assess the actual scale-dependent energy budget and deviations from the ΛCDM background.
AI.method: The authors employ a covariant scalar averaging formalism applied to the Cosmicflows-4++ reconstruction of the local Universe. They extract domain-averaged density, expansion rate, spatial curvature, and kinematical backreaction over cosmologically relevant domains extending up to a comoving radius of 300 Mpc/h around our Galaxy.
AI.result: The domain-averaged present-day energy budget shows nontrivial scale-dependent variations reflecting nested cosmic structures, including a large-scale void shell. Spatial curvature contributes at the 𝒪(10%) level on all probed scales, while kinematical backreaction is much smaller, reaching at most 𝒪(1%) on the smallest scales (30 Mpc/h). Convergence to the global ΛCDM background is not observed within the surveyed range.
AI.conclusion: Spatial curvature is a significant component of the local energy budget at the tens-of-percent level, whereas kinematical backreaction is negligible. The local Universe does not converge to the ΛCDM background within 300 Mpc/h, indicating that averaging effects and curvature are important for interpreting local cosmological measurements.

title: Differences between emission and absorption tracers of spatially resolved outflows in clumpy z ~ 0.1 star-forming galaxies
summary: We present spatially resolved Keck/LRIS spectroscopy of three clumpy star-forming galaxies at $z\sim0.1$, comparing outflow properties traced by H$α$ and Mg II emission with those probed by Mg II and Na I D absorption. Outflow velocities measured using Mg II absorption ($\langle v_{\rm out} \rangle = -560 \pm 30$~\kms) are consistently higher than those traced by H$α$ emission ($\langle v_{\rm out} \rangle = -124 \pm 3$~\kms) across $\sim$5 kpc$^{2}$ regions. Despite this offset, the correlation between $v_{\rm out}$ and galaxy properties, such as SFR and $Σ_{\rm SFR}$, show similar slopes for both tracers, with Mg II absorption systematically offset by $\sim 0.4$ dex. In two galaxies, Mg II emission is also detected, yielding velocities consistent with H$α$. In one galaxy we also detect outflows in Na I D absorption and find similar velocities as Mg II in absorption, which leads to a $\sim$0.4 dex higher Na I D outflow velocities compared to those measured in emission. Our spatially resolved results are consistent with those found for galactic-scale measurements, implying the outflow relationships are similar from the sales of $\sim$1-2 kpc to global measurements. Combined with literature measurements, these results suggest that the offset in velocities is driven not by ionisation state, but rather by the systematics associated to how absorption and emission measures trace the gas density.

AI.tldr: Using spatially resolved spectroscopy of three z~0.1 clumpy star-forming galaxies, this study finds that outflow velocities measured via Mg II and Na I D absorption are systematically ~0.4 dex higher than those traced by Hα and Mg II emission, with consistent scaling relations relative to SFR and Σ_SFR across ~1-2 kpc to global scales, suggesting the offset is due to methodological systematics in how absorption versus emission trace gas density rather than ionization state.
AI.motivation: To understand the systematic discrepancies between outflow velocity measurements derived from different tracers (absorption vs. emission) and to determine whether these offsets arise from ionization effects or methodological differences in how absorption and emission trace gas density.
AI.method: Spatially resolved Keck/LRIS spectroscopy of three clumpy star-forming galaxies at z~0.1, comparing outflow properties across ~5 kpc² regions using Hα and Mg II emission versus Mg II and Na I D absorption, with analysis of correlations between v_out and galaxy properties (SFR, Σ_SFR).
AI.result: Mg II absorption yields consistently higher outflow velocities (~-560 km/s) than Hα emission (~-124 km/s); correlation slopes with SFR and Σ_SFR are similar, with a systematic ~0.4 dex offset; Mg II emission velocities match Hα; Na I D absorption velocities match Mg II absorption, both ~0.4 dex higher than emission measures; spatially resolved results agree with galactic-scale measurements.
AI.conclusion: The systematic velocity offset between absorption and emission tracers is not driven by ionization state but by how absorption and emission methods differentially trace gas density, and these relationships hold consistently from ~1-2 kpc to global scales.

title: Self-interacting dark matter and core formation in field low-surface-brightness galaxies
summary: Dark matter may play an important role in galaxy formation through its non-trivial properties. For example, self-interacting dark matter may contribute to the formation of the widely observed core structures in galaxies. However, galaxy formation is a complex process, and such core structures can also arise from baryonic effects within the cold dark matter framework. To clarify the role of dark matter self-interactions, it is necessary to study systems that evolve without significant baryonic disturbances. Low-surface-brightness galaxies in the field, which are gravitationally isolated and have evolved with minimal external influence, are suitable candidates for this purpose. Since these galaxies typically contain only a small amount of baryonic matter, strong baryonic effects are not expected in their evolutionary history. In this study, we assume that these galaxies decoupled from proto-clusters at high redshift. Based on this assumption, we set initial conditions and estimate the time required for core formation, which we compare with the time corresponding to the redshift of proto-clusters. We examine five low-surface-brightness galaxies in the field and three observed proto-clusters at redshifts z=2.45, 7.66 and 7.88. Our analyses, based on order-of-magnitude estimates without numerical simulations, excludes a self-interaction cross section of sigma/m = 1 cm^2/g, while sigma/m = 0.1 cm^2/g is favored. This result is consistent with constraints derived from the shapes of present-day cluster cores.

AI.tldr: This paper uses low-surface-brightness field galaxies and high-redshift proto-clusters to constrain dark matter self-interaction cross sections, favoring σ/m = 0.1 cm²/g over 1 cm²/g based on order-of-magnitude estimates of core formation timescales, consistent with cluster core shape constraints.
AI.motivation: To disentangle whether core structures in galaxies arise from dark matter self-interactions or baryonic effects, the authors seek systems with minimal baryonic disturbances. Low-surface-brightness field galaxies, being baryon-poor and gravitationally isolated, are ideal for isolating the role of self-interacting dark matter.
AI.method: The authors assume these galaxies decoupled from proto-clusters at high redshift, set initial conditions based on this assumption, and estimate core formation timescales via order-of-magnitude calculations (without numerical simulations). They compare these timescales with the ages of three observed proto-clusters at z=2.45, 7.66, and 7.88, examining five low-surface-brightness field galaxies.
AI.result: A self-interaction cross section of σ/m = 1 cm²/g is excluded, while σ/m = 0.1 cm²/g is favored.
AI.conclusion: The favored cross section is consistent with constraints derived from present-day cluster core shapes, supporting the self-interacting dark matter interpretation for core formation in these minimally baryonic systems.

title: From Scalar $H_0$ to $E(z)$: A Reformulation of the Hubble Tension
summary: The Hubble tension is usually expressed as a discrepancy between the low H_0 inferred from Planck CMB data within base \LambdaCDM and the higher value obtained from late-time distance-ladder measurements. This scalar comparison compresses distinct inference problems into one derived parameter: Planck CMB, DESI DR2 BAO, and Pantheon+SH0ES constrain physical densities and acoustic scales, ruler-normalized distances, and calibrated luminosity-distance relations, respectively. We reformulate the comparison in terms of the dimensionless expansion history E(z)=H(z)/H_0. This does not remove the absolute-scale discrepancy, but separates the normalization encoded in $H_0$ from the redshift-dependent shape of the expansion history. Within a common flat-\LambdaCDM framework, each probe posterior is mapped onto posterior-implied E(z) histories. Since the reconstructed values E(z_k) are strongly correlated across redshift, we quantify the global mismatch with a covariance-subspace history displacement S_{hist}, alongside pointwise redshift differences. The histories are not identical, but the discrepancies are moderate: the pointwise significance is typically 1-2σ, while S_{hist} simeq 1.65 for DESI DR2 and S_{hist} \simeq 2.55 for Pantheon+SH0ES relative to Planck. With two retained covariance eigenmodes, these correspond to two-sided one-dimensional Gaussian equivalents of approximately 1.1σand 2.1σ, both below the conventional \simeq 4.9σPlanck-SH0ES scalar-H_0 discrepancy.

AI.tldr: This paper reformulates the Hubble tension by comparing expansion history E(z)=H(z)/H₀ across Planck CMB, DESI DR2 BAO, and Pantheon+SH0ES data. Using covariance-subspace displacement metrics, they find the shape discrepancies are only ~1.1-2.1σ, far below the ~4.9σ scalar H₀ tension, showing the tension is concentrated in the absolute normalization rather than the redshift-dependent expansion shape.
AI.motivation: The Hubble tension is typically quantified as a scalar discrepancy in H₀ between early and late-time probes. This compression masks how different datasets constrain different aspects of the expansion history. The authors seek to disentangle constraints on the normalization (H₀) from constraints on the shape of E(z) to better localize the origin of the tension.
AI.method: The authors map posterior distributions from Planck, DESI DR2 BAO, and Pantheon+SH0ES onto implied E(z)=H(z)/H₀ histories within flat ΛCDM. They quantify mismatches using a covariance-subspace displacement statistic S_hist that accounts for strong redshift correlations, alongside pointwise redshift differences.
AI.result: Pointwise discrepancies are typically 1-2σ. S_hist is ≈1.65 for DESI DR2 vs Planck and ≈2.55 for Pantheon+SH0ES vs Planck. When accounting for two covariance eigenmodes, these correspond to ~1.1σ and ~2.1σ equivalent one-dimensional Gaussian tensions, far below the conventional ~4.9σ H₀ tension.
AI.conclusion: The Hubble tension is primarily a discrepancy in the absolute scale/normalization (H₀) rather than in the shape of the expansion history E(z). The shape of the expansion history across probes shows only mild tension, indicating that the problem is concentrated in the calibration of absolute distances or the physics setting the sound horizon scale.

title: Axion-Like Particle Dark Matter Intensity Mapping: A New Probe via Cross-Correlation with Galaxy Surveys
comment: 9 pages, 5 figures, two tables. Accepted for publication in PLB
summary: The particle nature of dark matter (DM) remains one of the most significant enigmas in modern cosmology. Axion-like particles (ALPs), as well-motivated candidates for cold dark matter, can undergo radiative decay into photon pairs, a process that is significantly enhanced in the presence of ambient radiation fields. In this work, we propose a novel probe of $μ{\rm eV}$-scale ALP DM by cross-correlating radio intensity mapping (IM) with the large-scale galaxy distribution from the 2MASS Redshift Survey (2MRS) in the local universe ($z\leq 0.1$). We develop a comprehensive theoretical framework that incorporates stimulated decay effects driven by both the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) and a bottom-up modeled extragalactic radio background (ERB). By forecasting the sensitivity of the Square Kilometre Array (SKA) Phase 2, we demonstrate that this cross-correlation technique provides a promising and complementary approach to searching for ALP DM signals. This study establishes a new proof-of-concept for utilizing next-generation radio telescopes to probe ALP dark matter on cosmic scales.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes using cross-correlation between radio intensity mapping (SKA Phase 2) and galaxy surveys (2MRS) to detect μeV-scale axion-like particle dark matter via stimulated radiative decay enhanced by CMB and extragalactic radio backgrounds.
AI.motivation: The particle nature of dark matter remains unknown; axion-like particles are well-motivated candidates but detecting them directly is challenging, motivating the need for complementary probes on cosmic scales.
AI.method: Cross-correlate radio intensity mapping (IM) with the 2MASS Redshift Survey (2MRS) galaxy distribution at z ≤ 0.1, incorporating stimulated decay of ALPs driven by CMB and a bottom-up modeled extragalactic radio background (ERB).
AI.result: Forecasts show that SKA Phase 2 cross-correlation can probe μeV-scale ALP dark matter, providing a promising and complementary detection approach.
AI.conclusion: This work establishes a proof-of-concept that next-generation radio telescopes can probe ALP dark matter on cosmological scales via cross-correlation techniques.

title: Revisiting the Constancy of the Speed of Light: Galaxy Cluster Mass Bias Implications
comment: 8 pages, 3 figures, 2 tables. Paper published in Astroparticle Physics (180, 2026, 103249)
summary: In recent years, improvements in galaxy cluster observations have enabled a variety of tests of fundamental physics using these systems. In this work, we test the constancy of the speed of light, $c$, by combining X-ray gas mass fraction measurements from galaxy clusters with SNe Ia luminosity distance measurements from Pantheon+. We adopt the SH0ES prior on $H_0$ and the $Ω_b/Ω_m$ ratio from galaxy clustering observations, thereby minimizing the dependence of our analysis on any specific cosmological model. We explore different assumptions for the cluster mass calibration (mass bias), including \textsc{CLASH}, \textsc{CCCP}, and Planck-based estimates. We find no deviation from a constant $c$ when adopting \textsc{CLASH} or \textsc{CCCP} priors, while Planck-based calibration yields a mild tension, with the hypothesis of constant $c$ being only marginally consistent at the $2σ$ level, indicating a non-negligible sensitivity of the results to the adopted calibration scheme.

AI.tldr: This paper tests the constancy of the speed of light by combining X-ray gas mass fraction measurements from galaxy clusters with SNe Ia distance data, finding no deviation when using CLASH or CCCP calibrations, but marginal tension at 2σ with Planck-based calibration.
AI.motivation: To test the fundamental physics assumption of a constant speed of light using improved galaxy cluster observations combined with supernova data, while minimizing cosmological model dependence.
AI.method: Combined X-ray gas mass fraction measurements from galaxy clusters with SNe Ia luminosity distances from Pantheon+, adopted SH0ES prior on H₀ and Ω_b/Ω_m ratio from galaxy clustering, and tested three cluster mass calibration assumptions (CLASH, CCCP, Planck-based).
AI.result: No deviation from constant c found with CLASH or CCCP priors; Planck-based calibration yields a mild 2σ tension, showing sensitivity to the adopted calibration scheme.
AI.conclusion: The constancy of the speed of light is consistent with data under CLASH and CCCP calibrations, but results are noticeably sensitive to the choice of mass bias calibration, with Planck-based priors showing marginal inconsistency.

title: Chemical composition and kinematics of ionised gas in low-mass star-forming galaxies with extremely high [OIII]/[OII] ratios
comment: 20 pages, 13 figures, accepted for publication in Astronomy and Astrophysics
summary: We present Very Large Telescope/Xshooter spectrophotometric observations of eleven low-redshift (z<0.085) compact star-forming galaxies (`high O32 sample'). These galaxies are characterised by extremely high emission-line ratios [OIII]$λ$5007/[OII]3727, ranging from 11 to 42. Galaxies with such high ratios are thought to be promising candidates for leaking large amounts of Lyman continuum radiation. They are characterized by low oxygen abundances 12+log(O/H)\,=7.5-8.0 and low stellar masses M*~10^6-10^8 Msun. Strong emission lines of various ions in all spectra are used to derive helium and oxygen abundances, and N/O, Ne/O, S/O, Cl/O, Ar/O and Fe/O abundance ratios. We also derived macroscopic velocity dispersions sigma(lambda) from various emission lines of different ions. We find that sigma(4861) of the Hbeta emission line is increased with increasing stellar mass and decreasing O32 ratio. On the other hand, sigma(lambda)/sigma(4861) ratios for various lines are close to 1. Exceptions are sigma(lambda)/sigma(4861) of two lines, HeII 4686 and HeI 10830, which are considerably higher than unity and of four lines, [OII] 3726,3729, [SII] 6717,6731, with sigma(lambda)/sigma(4861) lower than unity. The two former lines are likely produced in the inner parts of HII regions and are broadened by dynamical processes generated by massive stars, and by radiative scattering in the case of the HeI 10830 emission line. Emission in the four latter lines is produced mainly in the outer and likely more quiet parts of HII regions.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes 11 compact star-forming galaxies with extremely high [OIII]/[OII] ratios (11-42), finding they are low-metallicity (12+log(O/H)=7.5-8.0), low-mass (10^6-10^8 Msun) systems that are promising Lyman continuum leakers. Velocity dispersion measurements show Hβ increases with mass and decreasing O32 ratio; HeII 4686 and HeI 10830 are broader than unity (originating in inner HII regions), while [OII] 3726,3729 and [SII] 6717,6731 are narrower (outer HII regions).
AI.motivation: To characterize compact star-forming galaxies with extreme [OIII]/[OII] ratios as candidate Lyman continuum leakers, deriving their chemical abundances and kinematic properties from emission lines.
AI.method: VLT/Xshooter spectrophotometric observations of 11 low-redshift (z<0.085) compact star-forming galaxies; measured emission lines to derive helium/oxygen abundances and abundance ratios (N/O, Ne/O, S/O, Cl/O, Ar/O, Fe/O); derived velocity dispersions σ(λ) from various emission lines.
AI.result: Galaxies have low oxygen abundances (7.5-8.0) and low stellar masses (10^6-10^8 Msun). σ(Hβ) increases with stellar mass and decreasing O32 ratio. σ(λ)/σ(4861) ≈ 1 for most lines, except HeII 4686 and HeI 10830 (>1, inner HII regions) and [OII] 3726,3729 and [SII] 6717,6731 (<1, outer HII regions).
AI.conclusion: The observed kinematic differences indicate that high-ionization lines (HeII, HeI) originate in turbulent inner HII regions driven by massive stars, while low-ionization lines ([OII], [SII]) form in quieter outer regions, consistent with these galaxies being promising Lyman continuum leakers.

title: Galaxy clusters in the LoTSS-DR3: Catalogues and detection pipeline for diffuse radio emission
comment: 14 pages, 8 figures, 2 tables, accepted by A&A
summary: The third data release of the LOFAR Two-metre Sky Survey provides an unprecedented view of the northern sky at 144 MHz. While compact sources can be efficiently identified with automated software packages, the detection of diffuse radio emission associated with galaxy clusters still requires dedicated processing and visual inspection. Given the scale of current and forthcoming radio surveys, automated approaches based on artificial intelligence are becoming essential to the identification of the most interesting targets. We aim to develop an automated pipeline to construct a catalogue of galaxy clusters hosting diffuse radio emission from LoTSS-DR3 20arcsec images. The pipeline is designed to provide both the probability that a cluster hosts diffuse radio emission and an interpretable image of its shape and morphology. We employed Radio U-Net, a convolutional neural network optimised for image segmentation (i.e. pixel-level identification) of diffuse radio emission. To associate detected emission with individual clusters, we combined the network output with positional, mass, and redshift information from four X-ray- and Sunyaev-Zeldovich-selected cluster catalogues, resulting in a merged sample of 3822 clusters covered by the LoTSS-DR3. We produced a pixel-level segmentation map of the full LoTSS-DR3 and a quantitative indicator for the presence of diffuse emission in each cluster. This enables the selection of sub-samples with specific properties for targeted follow-up or statistical studies. As a demonstration of the first application, we identified a sub-sample of 357 clusters selected at the highest network accuracy (76%), and we showed some examples of newly detected systems. For the second, using a larger statistical sample, we verified that the detection fraction of diffuse radio sources in the four catalogues increases with the mass and redshift of the clusters. [Abridged]

AI.tldr: This paper presents an automated pipeline using a convolutional neural network (Radio U-Net) to detect diffuse radio emission in galaxy clusters from LOFAR Two-metre Sky Survey (LoTSS-DR3) data, producing a catalogue of 3822 clusters with probability and morphological maps of diffuse emission, enabling both targeted follow-up and statistical studies.
AI.motivation: Current and forthcoming radio surveys produce data at scales that make manual detection of diffuse radio emission in galaxy clusters infeasible, necessitating automated AI-based approaches to efficiently identify interesting targets.
AI.method: Radio U-Net (a convolutional neural network for image segmentation) was applied to LoTSS-DR3 20arcsec images to identify diffuse radio emission at the pixel level. The network output was combined with positional, mass, and redshift data from four X-ray- and SZ-selected cluster catalogues, yielding a merged sample of 3822 clusters.
AI.result: A pixel-level segmentation map of the full LoTSS-DR3 was produced with a quantitative indicator of diffuse emission per cluster. A high-confidence sub-sample of 357 clusters (76% network accuracy) was identified, including newly detected systems. Statistical analysis confirmed that detection fraction increases with cluster mass and redshift.
AI.conclusion: The automated pipeline successfully enables both targeted (high-accuracy sub-sample selection) and statistical (mass/redshift scaling relations) studies of diffuse radio emission in galaxy clusters, demonstrating the viability of AI-driven approaches for large radio surveys.

title: The 2MIG isolated AGNs. 3. Optical--IR variability and dust reverberation in the NLSy1 galaxies Mrk~42 and Mrk~493
summary: This work presents the first dedicated optical--mid-infrared time-domain variability and dust-reverberation analysis of the isolated NLSy1 galaxies Mrk 42 and Mrk 493. We combine ZTF optical light curves, WISE mid-infrared monitoring, archival Swift and SDSS data, and high-cadence IAC80 optical observations. Using colour--magnitude relations, flux--flux analysis, and interpolated cross-correlation functions, we trace variable optical continuum and delayed dust response. Both galaxies show positive optical--MIR lags consistent with dust reverberation. For Mrk 493, we measure an observed-frame g--W1 lag of $τ_{\rm obs}=79.4\pm2.2$ d, corresponding to $R_{\rm dust}(W1)\simeq0.0648$ pc. For Mrk 42, the corresponding lag is $τ_{\rm obs}=39.1\pm2.6$ d, giving $R_{\rm dust}(W1)\simeq0.0320$ pc. These lags provide optical--MIR dust-reverberation radii and BLR--dust scale comparisons for both objects; the resulting $R_{\rm dust}/R_{\rm BLR}$ ratios are $\simeq6.8$ for Mrk 493 and $\sim6$--7 for Mrk 42. For Mrk 42, we derive the first host-subtracted AGN continuum luminosity at 5100 Å from SDSS spectral decomposition, giving a self-consistent BLR--dust comparison on an AGN-only luminosity basis. Both galaxies have similar radial hierarchies but different colour behaviour: Mrk 493 shows significant optical and MIR bluer-when-brighter trends, whereas Mrk 42 shows strong optical but weak MIR colour variability. We also identify and analyse a major optical flare in Mrk 42 with four internal maxima spaced by 45--47 d. We interpret this signal as quasi-periodic substructure within a broader accretion-driven flare, rather than as a strictly coherent periodic process. These results indicate that, even in dynamically isolated environments, the variability of low-mass, high-accretion-rate AGNs is governed mainly by the intrinsic state of the accretion flow and its coupling to circumnuclear dust.

AI.tldr: This paper presents the first dedicated optical–mid-infrared variability and dust-reverberation analysis of two isolated narrow-line Seyfert 1 galaxies, Mrk 42 and Mrk 493, measuring dust lags (~39 d and ~79 d) and finding R_dust/R_BLR ratios of ~6–7, with contrasting colour variability and a quasi-periodic flare in Mrk 42.
AI.motivation: To characterize the optical–MIR dust-reverberation properties and accretion–dust coupling in isolated NLSy1 galaxies, which are low-mass, high-accretion-rate AGNs with minimal environmental disturbance.
AI.method: Multi-wavelength time-domain analysis using ZTF optical, WISE mid-infrared, Swift, SDSS, and IAC80 data; colour–magnitude relations, flux–flux analysis, and interpolated cross-correlation functions to measure dust lags and variability trends.
AI.result: Mrk 493: observed g–W1 lag ~79.4 d (R_dust ~0.0648 pc); Mrk 42: lag ~39.1 d (R_dust ~0.0320 pc). R_dust/R_BLR ratios ~6–7. Mrk 493 shows bluer-when-brighter in both optical and MIR; Mrk 42 shows strong optical but weak MIR colour variability. A quasi-periodic flare with ~45–47 d spacing is identified in Mrk 42.
AI.conclusion: Even in isolated environments, the variability of low-mass, high-accretion-rate AGNs is primarily governed by the intrinsic accretion flow state and its coupling to circumnuclear dust, not by external environmental factors.

authors: the LSST Dark Energy Science Collaboration
title: Constraining Galaxy Cluster Triaxiality via Weak Lensing -- I. Preparation for the Rubin Data Beyond Leading Order
comment: 31 pages, 14 figures, 3 tables. Submitted to ApJ
summary: The 3D mass distributions of galaxy clusters are generally triaxial, a geometry that is difficult to constrain from projected observations. In this work, we measure the projected halo shapes of clusters from their weak lensing signatures using the triaxiality functionality in the Cluster Lensing Mass Modeling software, a tool developed by the Dark Energy Science Collaboration to analyze data from NSF-DOE Rubin Observatory's Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST). We measure ensemble halo ellipticity on the plane of the sky via axis-aligned stacking and multipole expansion of the weak lensing data. We study a precursor dataset -- the redMaPPer cluster catalog, the metacalibration shape catalog, and the Directional Neighborhood Fitting photometric redshift catalog from the Dark Energy Survey Year 3 public data release. We select clusters that have a high centering probability (>90%) of the identified central galaxy, and use the satellite galaxy distribution to determine the major-axis orientation for stacking. We extend the analysis to the second order of ellipticity in the monopole and quadrupole measurement. The projected ellipticity of the cluster sample is found to be $0.310^{+0.017}_{-0.016}$ (axis ratio $0.527^{+0.018}_{-0.019}$). The projected cluster ellipticity shows no statistically significant dependence on mass and redshift. We further verify the accuracy of the cluster shape measurement using mock catalogs. This analysis is applicable to datasets from upcoming wide-area cosmic surveys such as LSST, Euclid, and the Roman Space Telescope, where larger sample sizes will lead to tighter constraints on the cluster ellipticities.

AI.tldr: Using weak lensing and the Cluster Lensing Mass Modeling software, we measure the projected shapes of galaxy clusters from DES Y3 data, finding a mean ellipticity of 0.310 (axis ratio 0.527) with no significant mass or redshift dependence, validated with mock catalogs and applicable to future surveys like LSST, Euclid, and Roman.
AI.motivation: Galaxy clusters are triaxial, making it difficult to constrain their 3D mass distributions from projected observations; measuring projected halo shapes is essential for understanding cluster structure and cosmology.
AI.method: We used the triaxiality functionality in the Cluster Lensing Mass Modeling (CLMM) software to measure projected halo shapes via weak lensing. We performed axis-aligned stacking and multipole expansion (monopole and quadrupole up to second-order ellipticity) using DES Y3 data: redMaPPer cluster catalog, metacalibration shape catalog, and DNF photometric redshift catalog. Clusters with >90% centering probability were selected, and satellite galaxy distribution determined the major-axis orientation for stacking.
AI.result: The projected ellipticity of the cluster sample is 0.310 (+0.017/-0.016), corresponding to an axis ratio of 0.527 (+0.018/-0.019). No statistically significant dependence on mass or redshift was found. The measurement accuracy was verified using mock catalogs.
AI.conclusion: This weak lensing-based shape measurement method is validated and applicable to upcoming wide-area surveys (LSST, Euclid, Roman Space Telescope), where larger samples will yield tighter constraints on cluster ellipticities.

title: Photometric Redshift PDFs via Neural Network Classification for DESI Legacy Imaging Surveys and Pan-STARRS
comment: 19 pages, 8 figures, accepted for publication in The Astrophysical Journal Supplement Series. Data available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.18410731
summary: We present a neural network classification (NNC) method for photometric redshift estimation that produces well-calibrated redshift probability density functions (PDFs). The method discretizes the redshift space into ordered bins and optimizes the Continuous Ranked Probability Score (CRPS), which respects the ordinal nature of redshift and naturally provides uncertainty quantification. Unlike traditional regression approaches that output single point estimates, our method can capture multi-modal posterior distributions arising from color-redshift degeneracies. We apply this method to the DESI Legacy Imaging Surveys Data Release 10 (LSDR10) and Pan-STARRS Data Release 2 (PS1DR2), using an unprecedented spectroscopic training sample from DESI DR1 and SDSS DR19. Our method achieves $σ_{\mathrm{NMAD}} = 0.0153$ and $η= 0.50\%$ on LSDR10, and $σ_{\mathrm{NMAD}} = 0.0222$ and $η= 0.34\%$ on PS1DR2 combined with unWISE infrared photometry. The NNC method outperforms Random Forest, XGBoost, and standard neural network regression. We demonstrate that DESI DR1 significantly improves photo-$z$ performance at $z > 1$, while the combination of deep optical photometry and mid-infrared coverage is essential for achieving high precision across the full redshift range. We provide a unified photometric redshift catalog combining LSDR10 and PS1DR2 with a hierarchical model selection strategy based on available photometry. The well-calibrated PDFs produced by our method are valuable for cosmological studies and can be extended to next-generation surveys such as CSST, Euclid, and LSST.

AI.tldr: A neural network classification method for photometric redshift estimation that optimizes CRPS to produce well-calibrated PDFs, achieving state-of-the-art results on LSDR10 and PS1DR2 with DESI DR1 spectroscopic data.
AI.motivation: Traditional photometric redshift methods produce point estimates that cannot capture multi-modal posterior distributions from color-redshift degeneracies, and they often lack well-calibrated uncertainty quantification needed for cosmological studies.
AI.method: A neural network classification approach discretizes redshift into ordered bins and optimizes the Continuous Ranked Probability Score (CRPS) to respect ordinal structure and provide probabilistic outputs. Applied to LSDR10 and PS1DR2 with DESI DR1 + SDSS DR19 spectroscopic training samples, combined with unWISE infrared photometry for PS1DR2.
AI.result: Achieves σ_NMAD = 0.0153 and η = 0.50% on LSDR10; σ_NMAD = 0.0222 and η = 0.34% on PS1DR2 + unWISE. Outperforms Random Forest, XGBoost, and standard neural network regression. DESI DR1 significantly improves photo-z at z > 1; deep optical + mid-IR coverage essential for full-range precision.
AI.conclusion: The NNC method produces well-calibrated PDFs valuable for cosmology and extensible to next-generation surveys (CSST, Euclid, LSST). A unified photometric redshift catalog combining LSDR10 and PS1DR2 is provided via hierarchical model selection.

title: The Pulsar Radial Acceleration Relation
summary: The radial acceleration relation (RAR) links observed and baryonic accelerations, and is best established in rotation curves of late-type galaxies. Pulsar timing, which measures line-of-sight (LOS) differential accelerations between the Sun and pulsars, provides a novel probe of this relation, including along directions outside the Galactic disc. By combining these pulsar differential accelerations with the acceleration at the Sun, we test whether current pulsar timing data carry information on a vector generalisation of the RAR, ${g}_{\rm obs}=ν(|{g}_{\rm bar}|){g}_{\rm bar}$. Comparing the measured SPARC RAR (generalised to 3D) to 26 binary-system pulsars with literature accelerations, we find a reduced $χ^2$ of 3.58, compared with 10.86 for Newtonian baryonic gravity alone. However, setting all accelerations to that of the Sun gives a reduced $χ^2$ of 3.75, showing that this vector RAR test is dominated by the Solar acceleration with current data.

AI.tldr: This paper tests the vector generalization of the radial acceleration relation (RAR) using pulsar timing data, finding that while the RAR fits better (reduced χ²=3.58) than Newtonian baryonic gravity alone (reduced χ²=10.86), the test is dominated by the Solar acceleration as setting all accelerations to that of the Sun yields a similar reduced χ² of 3.75.
AI.motivation: To test the radial acceleration relation (RAR) in directions outside the Galactic disc using pulsar timing data, providing a novel probe of this relation beyond traditional rotation curve measurements of late-type galaxies.
AI.method: Combined pulsar differential accelerations (line-of-sight differential accelerations between the Sun and pulsars) with the acceleration at the Sun to test a vector generalization of the RAR (g_obs = ν(|g_bar|)g_bar), comparing the SPARC RAR generalized to 3D against 26 binary-system pulsars with literature accelerations.
AI.result: The vector RAR test gives a reduced χ² of 3.58 for the SPARC RAR, compared to 10.86 for Newtonian baryonic gravity alone. However, a model setting all accelerations to that of the Sun yields a reduced χ² of 3.75, indicating the test is dominated by the Solar acceleration with current data.
AI.conclusion: Current pulsar timing data carry limited independent information for testing the vector RAR beyond the Solar acceleration; improved data are needed for a more constraining test.
